issues.legal_issue: A Letters Patent Bench reviewing a factual finding in an appeal from a first appeal may interfere with concurrent findings only on a demonstrable and serious error.
material_facts: The Trial Court and the Single Judge both found that the will had been proved.
The Letters Patent Appeal arose from the Single Judge’s decision in a first appeal, and the Division Bench reversed the finding on the basis of its assessment of the attesting witness’s evidence.
The Supreme Court held that the Division Bench had misread that evidence.
issues.conclusion: Although the Division Bench was not barred from examining the factual finding because the Single Judge had decided a first appeal, it should have interfered only if the finding was demonstrably erroneous, irrational, perverse, or unsupported by evidence. Its interference in this case was not justified.
issues.legal_principle: A Letters Patent Bench cannot reappreciate evidence when the Single Judge is exercising second-appellate jurisdiction, in view of Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. When the Single Judge has decided a first appeal, there is no express bar to examination of a factual finding, including a concurrent finding, but the Bench should be slow to interfere and must exercise its discretionary jurisdiction judicially. The Court relied on Smt. Asha Devi v. Dukhi Sao and Anr. (1974) 2 SCC 492 and B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh and Ors. (2006) 13 SCC 449.

rule.if: letters_patent_appeal_from_first_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and not demonstrable_error_in_findings

predicates.letters_patent_appeal_from_first_appeal: The proceeding is a Letters Patent Appeal from a decision made in a first appeal.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual finding.
predicates.demonstrable_error_in_findings: The factual finding is demonstrably irrational, perverse, or unsupported by evidence.

issues.definition: When a Letters Patent Appeal arises from a first appeal and the lower courts have concurrent factual findings, the Division Bench should not disturb those findings unless they contain a demonstrable error.

issues.legal_issue: An unprivileged will is proved when the evidence satisfies the statutory requirements for execution and attestation and persuades a prudent mind that it was duly executed.
material_facts: The dispute concerned an unprivileged will propounded to establish that the deceased testator’s property would pass to one beneficiary.
One of the two attesting witnesses was called and testified that the testator signed the will in his presence and that the other attesting witness was also present when the testator signed it.

The witness’s evidence established that both attesting witnesses signed in the testator’s presence; the statement that the other witness was present when the testator signed was not challenged in cross-examination.
The testator’s signature was placed at the bottom of the will in a manner indicating that the document was intended to operate as a will.
The will was registered, and the Court found no suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution.
issues.conclusion: The will’s execution was satisfactorily proved. The Division Bench erred in finding that the statutory requirements had not been met, and the Supreme Court restored the Single Judge’s decision.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, an unprivileged will must be signed by the testator, or by another person in the testator’s presence and at the testator’s direction; the signature must indicate an intention to give effect to the document as a will; and at least two witnesses must attest it in the prescribed manner, including signing in the testator’s presence. Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, at least one attesting witness must be called to prove execution when such a witness is available and capable of giving evidence. Registration does not dispense with proof of execution. The Court relied on Bhagwan Kaur v. Kartar Kaur (1994) 5 SCC 135, Seth Beni Chand v. Smt. Kamla Kunwar (1976) 4 SCC 554, Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam (2003) 2 SCC 91, Gurdev Kaur v. Kaki (2007) 1 SCC 546, Yumnam Ongbi Tampha Ibema Devi v. Yumnam Joykumar Singh (2009) 4 SCC 780, Rur Singh v. Bachan Kaur (2009) 11 SCC 1, Anil Kak v. Kumari Sharada Raje (2008) 7 SCC 695, and H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443. Proof need not reach mathematical certainty; it must satisfy the test of a prudent mind.

rule.if: unprivileged_will_proceeding and attesting_witness_examined and testator_signed_or_directed_signature and signature_indicates_will_intent and two_attesting_witnesses_proved and witnesses_signed_in_testator_presence and prudent_mind_satisfied

predicates.unprivileged_will_proceeding: The proceeding concerns proof of an unprivileged will.
predicates.attesting_witness_examined: At least one available and capable attesting witness was called to give evidence about execution.
predicates.testator_signed_or_directed_signature: The testator signed or marked the will, or another person signed it in the testator’s presence and at the testator’s direction.
predicates.signature_indicates_will_intent: The placement of the testator’s signature or mark indicates an intention to give effect to the writing as a will.
predicates.two_attesting_witnesses_proved: The evidence proves that at least two witnesses attested the will in a legally sufficient manner.
predicates.witnesses_signed_in_testator_presence: Each attesting witness signed the will in the testator’s presence.
predicates.prudent_mind_satisfied: The evidence, considered as a whole, satisfies a prudent mind that the will was duly executed.

issues.definition: When an unprivileged will proceeding includes proof of the testator’s signature, the intended testamentary effect of the document, the required attestation and signatures in the testator’s presence, and the evidence satisfies a prudent mind, the will’s execution is proved.
